Now let's discuss why capital works. We humans have two natures: an altruistic nature, where we care about human relationships and want to be nice to people, seeing them as part of our family; and a utilitarian nature, where we focus on goals, profit, money, and power. These two sides coexist within us.

When you go to a restaurant, if the meal is good, you pay a lot and tip generously. At home, when your mother cooks a nice meal and is happy to see you, you say thank you. The opposite would be inappropriate: saying "Thank you" at a restaurant but leaving without tipping or not expressing gratitude to your mother.

Capital moves us from an altruistic state to a utilitarian one. Initially, this shift is positive because altruism can lead to inaction and harmony, which may stagnate progress. In many villages, static conditions are preferred over change, as outsiders can be seen as threats to social systems.

When capital enters, it encourages work, innovation, and exploration. This growth is beneficial until the system reaches a point of maximum expansion, after which the utilitarian nature becomes excessive. Excessive utilitarianism leads to exploitation, cheating, and moral decay, eventually causing the system to collapse.

Similarly, in a group led by a person without capital, status, reputation, and feelings are prioritized over monetary gain. Once capital is introduced, leaders see their followers as commodities for exploitation, leading to alliances, conquests, and inequality. The few who accumulate wealth exploit the many below them, causing resentment and potential revolt.

Thus, capital can drive growth but also leads to collapse due to its inherent tendencies toward exploitation and inequality. This cycle explains why ancient civilizations like the Bronze Age rose and fell, just as our current world may experience similar dynamics.
